To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) knowledge about AIDS risk is a necessary but not sufficient condition for critical processing, and (b) the motivational orientation of the knowledgeable subject is an important determinant of the direction and extent of biased processing.

(1) attitude-relevant knowledge enables biased systematic processing of attitude-relevant information, (2) the extent to which this occurs depends on the affective intensity of the attitude, and (3) the affective intensity is a function of attitude-relevant knowledge.
attitude-relevant information processing was affected by the level of knowledge, the intensity of affect, and the congruence of the attitude-relevant information with the existing attitude.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cognitive processes underlying biased information processing and the determinants of biased processing.
the role of knowledge in the processing and evaluation of new information.
the role that working knowledge of a social problem (AIDS) plays in the processing and evaluation of new information about the problem.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the attitude-relevant knowledge of the subjects was a necessary, but not a sufficient, condition for the occurrence of biased processing.
the more knowledge a person has about AIDS risk and prevention, the more he or she will process AIDS risk information in a systematic and critical manner.
knowledge can be used to bolster or defend attitudes, but only when the knowledge is highly relevant, when the attitude is intense, and when the attitude is threatened.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
knowledge and attitudes interact to influence the processing and evaluation of new information in complex ways.
attitude-relevant working knowledge can enable either biased or objective systematic information processing.
the more knowledgeable subjects are about a topic the more likely it is that their attitudes will affect the way in which they process information about that topic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
knowledge can be used to bolster or to challenge existing attitudes, depending on the affective motivation of the individual.
the cognitive processing orientation of knowledgeable individuals depends on their affective reactions to the issue in question.
knowledge is not a panacea.
